item.title: Dengue surge raises questions over government preparedness
item.description:
Despite repeated outbreaks in previous years and access to historical data, Bangladesh has seen a sharp rise in dengue cases and deaths in 2026. While the seasonal surge during the monsoon is well known, questions have been raised over why effective preventive measures were not taken before infections began to climb.
Concerns have also emerged over whether timely mosquito-control operations and stronger preventive measures could have reduced the number of infections, as well as whether the health and local government ministries have coordinated effectively to prepare for and contain the outbreak. Although dengue cases and deaths in 2026 have increased significantly compared with 2025, the health and local government ministries have cited figures from 2023 to claim that the situation remains better than in previous years.
From January 1 to October 25, Bangladesh recorded 132,948 dengue infections and 384 deaths this year, according to figures cited in the report.
During the same period in 2025, the country recorded 64,297 cases and 259 deaths. In 2024, the figures stood at 54,702 cases and 269 deaths.
Compared with the corresponding period in 2025, dengue cases have increased by 106.8% this year, while deaths have risen by 48.3%. Compared with the same period in 2024, cases have increased by 143% and deaths by 42.8%.
However, the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) reported that 123,998 dengue patients were hospitalised between January 1 and October 25, with 384 deaths recorded during the period. The discrepancy between the total case figures cited above and the DGHS hospitalisation data requires verification.
Dhaka Division recorded the highest number of hospitalisations, with 50,292 patients and 183 deaths. Khulna Division ranked second, with 19,092 hospitalisations and 68 deaths.
Chittagong Division reported 18,261 hospitalisations and 37 deaths, while Barisal Division recorded 15,633 hospitalisations and 28 deaths.
Khulna, which ranks second after Dhaka in dengue cases and deaths, has continued mosquito-control and cleanliness drives to curb the outbreak.
Asked about the measures being taken, Khulna Civil Surgeon Dr Md Moniruzzaman said he had joined the post on October 15 and was implementing activities in line with directives from the Ministry of Local Government.
“We are conducting cleanliness drives in areas where stagnant water in ditches, drains and other places could create breeding grounds for Aedes mosquitoes. These drives continue every day, with intensified efforts on Saturdays,” he said.
He added that reports on the activities were being submitted to the ministry.
“We are coordinating with public and private schools, colleges and other institutions to continue mosquito-control operations,” he said, adding that his predecessor had also carried out similar initiatives.
Experts warn that once dengue begins spreading in an area, bringing the outbreak under control becomes difficult. However, regular mosquito-control operations, proper sanitation, the elimination of breeding grounds and timely public health interventions can help reduce transmission.
The rising number of cases has renewed questions about whether preventive measures were implemented early enough and whether coordination among the relevant authorities has been sufficient to contain the outbreak.
Entomologist Professor Kabirul Bashar said climate change is altering temperature, rainfall and humidity patterns in Bangladesh, affecting the spread of Aedes mosquitoes and the transmission of dengue.
He stressed the need to revise mosquito-control strategies to adapt to changing climatic conditions.
While climate change can be addressed through mitigation and adaptation, large-scale mitigation efforts may be beyond the capacity of agencies responsible for mosquito control. However, authorities can develop adaptation-based strategies by identifying how changes in weather and environmental conditions affect Aedes mosquito behaviour, he said.
Asked about preventive measures taken since the government assumed office, amid a rise in dengue cases and deaths compared with the same period last year despite the availability of historical data, State Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Mir Shahe Alam said preventive activities had been ongoing since the beginning of the government's tenure.
“Our responsibility is to take preventive measures, and we have been doing so since taking office. We have undertaken cleanliness drives, awareness campaigns and leaflet distribution,” he said.
He added that the government had decided to launch large-scale awareness campaigns through loudspeaker announcements across city corporations, municipalities, districts and upazilas.
The campaigns aim to raise public awareness and eliminate potential Aedes mosquito breeding grounds, he said.
The state minister also said anti-dengue activities were being conducted every Saturday with the participation of Scouts, Rover Scouts and voluntary organisations. The programme will continue every Saturday until December 12, he added.
Meanwhile, the government has decided to form 20 special monitoring committees across 20 zones of Dhaka North and Dhaka South city corporations to strengthen dengue prevention, improve cleanliness and eliminate mosquito breeding grounds.
Director-level officials from the Prime Minister's Office will lead the committees, which will include representatives from the relevant ministries, Dhaka WASA, the metropolitan police and the city corporations, as well as executive magistrates.
The committees will monitor dengue prevention efforts and oversee intensified cleanliness drives.
Public health expert Dr Mustak Hossain said dengue had become a persistent public health crisis in Bangladesh and could not be controlled through superficial fogging operations or fines alone.
He said the government should have formed a high-level interministerial task force, similar to the one established during the Covid-19 pandemic, and implemented the 2019 national dengue management guidelines at the grassroots level.
He recommended identifying a one-kilometre radius around each confirmed patient's location as a potential hotspot and launching targeted operations to destroy mosquito larvae in line with scientific guidelines.
He also stressed the need to encourage community participation at the ward level, following Kolkata's model, and provide free dengue tests and mosquito nets to low-income patients through public hospitals.
Unless the government adopts a scientific, source-based approach to eliminating mosquito larvae, the country will continue to pay a heavy price for the outbreak, he warned.
State Minister for Health Dr MA Mohit said dengue-prone areas were being identified for mosquito-larvae destruction and cleanliness drives.
Hospitals' patient records are being analysed to identify areas with high infection rates, where special cleanliness drives and larvicide applications are being carried out promptly, he said, adding that city corporations were also involved in the efforts.
“There is no shortage of government initiatives to tackle dengue,” he said.
According to the state minister, weekly meetings are being held with mayors, administrators and officials from the health and local government ministries to review the situation. The prime minister, ministers and state ministers are also discussing the issue regularly.
He claimed that collective efforts had kept the dengue infection rate lower this year than in previous years.
Five more people died of dengue and 1,546 new patients were hospitalized across the country in the 24 hours ending at 8:00am on Monday.
With the latest fatalities, the dengue death toll in the country has risen to 389 this year, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Among the new deaths, one each was reported in Dhaka, Chittagong, Khulna, Rajshahi and Barisal divisions.
Since January 1 this year, a total of 126,166 dengue patients have been admitted to hospitals across the country. Of them, 119,393 have recovered.

item.title: CPB office attacked in Paltan
item.description:
A group of people attacked Mukti Bhaban, the office of the Communist Party of Bangladesh (CPB), in Dhaka's Paltan area on Monday night.
The attack took place around 10pm.
The CPB blamed BNP and Jamaat-e-Islami activists for the incident, while BNP activists denied the allegation.
CPB Central Committee President Sazzad Zahir Chandan told Dhaka Tribune that a group of youths had launched a sudden attack on their office.
He blamed BNP and Jamaat activists for the attack, saying the situation stemmed from the detention and subsequent release of former Bangladesh Chhatra Union president Dipak Shil earlier in the evening.
According to Chandan, the attackers accused CPB activists of chanting “Joy Bangla”. He, however, said no such slogan had been chanted from the party office.
Officer-in-Charge of Paltan police station Ariful Islam told Dhaka Tribune that Dipak's supporters had chanted “Joy Bangla” in celebration after he was released from detention.
Angered by the slogans, some people attacked the CPB office, he said.
Police are investigating the incident and have positioned themselves between the two groups to prevent further unrest, he said.

item.title: Tarique, Takaichi to hold bilateral summit in Tokyo Tuesday
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is set to hold a bilateral summit with his Japanese counterpart, Sanae Takaichi, in Tokyo on Tuesday to strengthen the strategic partnership, boost trade and investment, and expand cooperation in key sectors between Bangladesh and Japan.
The meeting will begin at 11:45am local time at the Japanese Prime Minister’s Office, known as the Kantei, following a guard of honour to be given to Tarique Rahman from 11:30am to 11:40am.
The two leaders will hold talks until 12:10pm, followed by a joint press announcement from 12:15pm to 12:25pm.
Takaichi will then host a luncheon for the Bangladesh Prime Minister from 12:30pm to 1:10pm.
At the beginning of the lunch, she is scheduled to deliver a brief welcome remark and propose a toast, followed by a short reply and return toast from Tarique Rahman.
According to Prime Minister’s Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Hossain Shadhin, the two leaders will discuss strengthening bilateral relations, expanding business, trade and investment, Japanese cooperation in various sectors and international issues.
At a curtain-raiser press conference back in Dhaka, Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam said the Prime Minister’s four-day visit is expected to open new avenues for bilateral cooperation and attract fresh Japanese private investment in Bangladesh.
He said the talks would focus on the effective implementation of the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA), signed in February 2026, expanding access for Bangladeshi products to the Japanese market and strengthening business engagement.
The two sides are also expected to explore cooperation in renewable energy, agriculture, science and technology, digital transformation, skills development and human resource development.
Siam said several memorandums of understanding (MoUs) are being discussed for signing during the visit. Draft agreements cover agriculture, fisheries, human resource and skills development, domestic aviation, trade, environmental conservation and the modernisation of local government.
“We hope that many of these MoUs will be signed during the visit,” he said.
During the visit, Tarique Rahman is also scheduled to deliver the keynote address at the Japan-Bangladesh Economic Forum and meet Japanese business leaders.
The prime minister reached Tokyo on Monday morning on a four-day visit at the invitation of Takaichi.
He was received at Narita International Airport by Japanese State Minister for Foreign Affairs Nakasone Yasutaka.
Tarique Rahman is leading a high-level delegation that includes Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Finance and Planning Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir, State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit, and Prime Minister’s Adviser on Posts, Telecommunications, ICT and Science and Technology Rehan Asif Asad.

item.title: Karnaphuli Garden City shopping complex closes after business downturn
item.description:
Once a popular shopping destination in the capital, Karnaphuli Garden City has remained closed since October 1 amid a business downturn, declining customer numbers and mounting unpaid bills.
During a visit on Monday, the shopping complex's main entrance was found shut, with a banner announcing: “The shopping complex will remain closed from October 1, 2026.”
According to those concerned, the 20-storey building was established by Karnaphuli Group at the Shantinagar-Kakrail intersection in 1998. The shopping mall occupied the ground floor through the 3rd floor, while the 4th floor housed a food court and garden.
The complex initially had 198 shops. However, by the time it closed, only 17 shops inside the complex and 25 in total, including those outside, remained open.
Bakibillah Osmani, general secretary of the owners’ association, told Dhaka Tribune that the closure resulted from a decade of mismanagement, the country's economic downturn and a lack of business.
He said: “This did not happen in a single day. Whether you call it a decade of mismanagement, the country's economic downturn or a lack of business, all these factors have contributed to this situation over the past decade.”
He said the difficult period began around 2016–17, when the Shantinagar flyover was constructed. Some shop owners who also owned the businesses operating there moved to other markets, expecting to return if the complex reopened or road conditions improved.
According to him, road closures during flyover construction reduced customer numbers. Established businesses moved to other markets and did not return. The Covid-19 pandemic further worsened the situation.
He said: “When the market reopened, the traders did not return. They had settled in other markets. Then the pandemic, Covid, came. During that period, some traders closed their shops permanently. Gradually, the shops began to close. On the day we closed the market, only 17 shops inside were open. Including those outside, the total was 25.”
Describing the complex's financial situation, Bakibillah Osmani said monthly expenses, including electricity bills and staff salaries, exceeded Tk15 lakh.
He said: “We were receiving a maximum of Tk1 lakh to Tk1.5 lakh in service charges.”
The complex's outstanding electricity bills have reportedly exceeded Tk50 lakh.
He had previously said: “Service charges were not coming in, and the outstanding electricity bill had reached around Tk50 lakh. As a result, all the owners jointly decided to close the market.”
He also said the complex had been operating for more than 6 months using money borrowed from market committee officials and some of the owners.

item.title: Minister: Committee to probe freedom fighter’s burial in Pirojpur
item.description:
Liberation War Affairs Minister Ahmed Azam Khan has said a committee will be formed to investigate the incident in Pirojpur in which the wife and daughter of a freedom fighter allegedly dug up his grave and buried him.
He said those responsible would face appropriate action based on the findings of the investigation.
The minister made the remarks while responding to questions from journalists after visiting the Martyred Intellectuals Memorial in Rayerbazar, Dhaka, on Monday.
“I will look into the matter as soon as I return to my office today. I will also speak with the Muktijoddha Sangsad in Pirojpur. We will form a committee to investigate the incident and take appropriate action against those responsible based on the investigation report,” he said.
The minister said Bangladesh is an independent, democratic republic and there is no scope for anyone to take a position against the Liberation War.
He said the Liberation War Affairs Ministry had not been properly informed about the incident involving the freedom fighter.
“If the ministry had been informed, it could have taken the matter into consideration earlier and taken necessary steps,” he said.
Ahmed Azam Khan said some people opposed the Liberation War in 1971 and that he believed those forces remained active in the country.
“They are trying to advance their position through various tactics and, when given the opportunity, attempt to undermine the Liberation War by portraying different movements as a ‘second independence’,” he said.
The minister said the ministry has been working to thwart any conspiracy against the Liberation War and freedom fighters. “We are always prepared to deal with such situations,” he added.

item.title: Climate change leaves coastal elderly isolated
item.description:
In a small, dilapidated shelter beside a canal in Haoladar Bari of Pratapnagar union in Satkhira’s Ashashuni upazila, Shahjahan Ali, in his seventies, and his wife Rabeya Begum, in her sixties, spend their days gazing at the water that has destroyed their lives.
They once owned two bighas of land, a mango orchard, paddy fields and a well-maintained home. But Super Cyclone Amphan in May 2020 breached nearby embankments, allowing saline water from the Kholpetua and Kapatakkha rivers to inundate their homestead and farmland. Repeated flooding gradually destroyed their land and livelihoods.
As river erosion and salinity worsened, their adult sons left in search of work, taking their children with them.
“I miss my grandchildren, but what can we do? They have left in search of work. Where can we go at this age? We once had everything, including our loved ones. Now, there is nobody,” Rabeya said.
Her husband, Shahjahan Ali, recalled how his wife’s family once owned hundreds of bighas of land.
“I can no longer work because of my illness. Whatever our son gives us is not enough to run the household, and we often go hungry. I am tired of this lonely life. Now, I am simply waiting for death,” he said.
Their story reflects a growing crisis along Bangladesh’s southwestern coast, where climate-related disasters are destroying livelihoods, driving migration and leaving elderly people increasingly isolated.
Shamsun Nahar Ratna, a senior scientific officer at the Soil Resource Development Institute’s Satkhira regional office, said salinity in the Kholpetua River had risen from 22-25 decisiemens per metre in 2019 to as high as 50-55 in 2026.
According to Bangladesh’s 2024 Soil Salinity Map, around 1.16 million hectares of the country’s 1.70 million hectares of coastal agricultural land have become severely saline.
Ratna attributed the worsening situation partly to declining upstream river flows, irregular rainfall and the movement of saline water towards the soil surface. The resulting damage to farmland is pushing farmers towards fish and shrimp farming.
According to figures cited in the report, around 2.5 million people were displaced from coastal areas during Amphan in 2020. Data from the International Organization for Migration and the government indicate that approximately 4.96 million people are internally displaced by disasters such as floods, river erosion and storm surges. The World Bank has warned that Bangladesh could have nearly 20 million internal climate migrants by 2050 without effective action.
A joint survey by Satkhira municipality and development organisation Uttaran found that 10,133 families had moved to the district town over 22 years because of natural disasters. Around 84% had lost their homes to river erosion, storm surges and salinity.
Many now live in overcrowded settlements with inadequate housing, sanitation and drainage facilities.
In neighbouring Gabura union of Shyamnagar upazila, 60-year-old Fazila Khatun, a widow who is partially paralysed, struggles to survive after her children left in search of work.
“We used to live by farming. Now there is salt everywhere. Even a vegetable plant cannot survive. We have to walk miles to collect drinking water,” she said.
Environmental activist and researcher Piyush Baulia Pintu blamed repeated cyclones, unplanned shrimp farming and poorly planned sluice gates for weakening embankments. In parts of Gabura, including Durgabati, Harinnagar, Singhortali and Jelekhali, erosion has swallowed homes and entire settlements.
He said some displaced residents had taken out loans to buy vans or venture into unfamiliar occupations but were later forced to leave when they could not repay their debts.
Farida Parvin, a reserved-seat woman member of Gabura union parishad, said climate change, particularly persistent river erosion, tidal surges and severe cyclones, was the main driver of displacement in the area.
“Income-generating opportunities are also extremely limited. Previously, paddy cultivation provided jobs for around 20 labourers during the farming season. But saltwater fish and shrimp farming requires only one worker, leaving the other 19 unemployed and forcing them to leave the area,” she said.
Madhab Chandra Dutta, executive director of human rights organisation Swadesh, said climate change was also causing non-economic losses, including the erosion of cultural identity, mental well-being and social bonds.
Traditional practices such as boat races, folk songs and rituals associated with Bonbibi and Manasa are disappearing as people abandon their ancestral homes and traditional occupations.
Bhakta Munda, a resident of Datinakhali, said the struggle to survive had overshadowed cultural life.
“After Amphan and Yaas, people became so preoccupied with survival that the joy of festivals disappeared. Social bonds among neighbours are also fading,” he said.
Farida Parvin, a reserved-seat woman member of Gabura union parishad, said shrinking employment opportunities were accelerating migration.
“During the paddy cultivation season, around 20 labourers could find work in a field. But shrimp farming can often be managed by just one worker. The others are left without jobs and forced to leave,” she said.
According to Farida, around two in every 10 families in Gabura have relocated, while elderly parents are often left behind without independent sources of income.
Ashik-e-Elahi, convener of the Satkhira Climate Council, said climate change had become a human rights issue. He called for accessible loans and entrepreneurship support to help young people remain in agriculture, alongside greater investment in vulnerable communities.
Dutta urged authorities to build durable concrete-block embankments, rehabilitate displaced families on available government-owned land and create alternative employment opportunities.
Sonia Akter Pushpa, a psychosocial counsellor at Moner Bondhu, said migration was placing severe psychological pressure on women and elderly people left behind. She called for local employment opportunities, regular communication between family members and community-based mental health services.
Without sustained investment in embankments, rehabilitation, livelihoods and psychosocial support, experts warn, coastal communities risk losing not only their homes but also their cultural heritage and social bonds.

item.title: Police release former Chhatra Union president Dipak Shil
item.description:
Police have released Dipak Shil, former president of Bangladesh Chhatra Union, after detaining him during a human chain by artists and cultural activists at Dhanmondi 27 in the capital on Monday.
Officer-in-Charge (OC) of Mohammadpur Police Station Abdul Halim confirmed the matter on Monday night, saying Dipak was freed after questioning.
Chhatra Union Secretary Bahauddin Shuvo also confirmed it in a Facebook post around 9:00pm.
The human chain was organised under the banner of “Protesting Artists and People” to protest attacks on Baul music and other cultural events in different parts of the country in the name of “Tawhidi Janata”.
The programme was scheduled for Monday afternoon on Dhanmondi 27 Road, but police obstructed the gathering and detained Dipak.
Actress Sumana Soma, who attended the programme, said they had gathered to protest attacks on Bauls and obstruction of cultural events across the country.
“When police obstructed us, we protested. Police personnel then dragged us towards their vehicle, while Dipak was taken away in a police van,” she said.
Cultural activist Faruk H Khan condemned the cancellation of Baul music programmes, obstruction of protests by artists and citizens, and alleged interference with the namaz- e- janaza and burial of freedom fighter Manik Pashari.
He said Baul traditions and Bengali culture were facing continued attacks across the country. He also alleged that anti-liberation forces and militant fundamentalist groups were behind the incidents.

item.title: Curriculum reform and the old wounds of a new attempt
item.description:
Today's workforce demands a broad set of competencies: C ritical thinking, problem-solving, communication, empathy, collaboration, adaptability, entrepreneurship, strong reading and writing, digital literacy, and lifelong learning.
Not all of these need to be fully developed at school. Schools lay the foundations; universities and workplaces deepen them. Reading, writing, basic digital skills, communication, empathy and teamwork begin at school. Critical thinking and problem-solving are introduced there but mature later through more independent and open-ended work. Entrepreneurship and self-directed learning also develop through higher education and work experience.
That is the ideal division of labour . The question is whether Bangladeshi schools are laying those foundations.
The gap between design and classroom
Bangladesh has repeatedly tried to build a more competency-based curriculum. Each attempt has promised less rote memorization and more critical thinking and practical learning. But writing a curriculum is easier than delivering it across tens of thousands of schools.
The 2021 competency-based curriculum began to be introduced in 2023, with plans to extend it to Class XII by 2027. Yet even a well-designed curriculum cannot succeed on paper alone. Its success depends on teachers, resources and classroom conditions.
Studies of its implementation identified gaps between what the curriculum expected and what many classrooms could deliver. Teachers were not always adequately prepared. Schools differed greatly in facilities and resources, particularly between urban and rural areas. Teaching materials were sometimes lacking, while textbook delivery was repeatedly delayed.
Consider collaboration. Group work is difficult when one teacher must manage a large class with limited space and materials. Critical thinking is equally difficult to teach if teachers have not been trained to develop it.
Assessment may be the biggest obstacle. Students and families naturally organize their efforts around what is tested. If major examinations continue to reward memorization and reproduction of prepared answers, a competency-based curriculum will struggle to change how students learn.
After reviewing implementation difficulties, the interim government reverted to the previous curriculum in early 2025.
The lesson is clear: C hanging what students are expected to learn is not enough. Reform must also address how learning takes place in the classroom.
The 2026 initiative
The current government has launched another curriculum reform, with a broader overhaul planned for 2028. The government says it is moving more gradually than the previous reform. It has also announced new elements including sports, culture, technical and vocational education, and “Learning with Happiness . ” More recent government statements have also highlighted AI, robotics, machine learning and cybersecurity.
These are useful directions. But they raise a more fundamental question: What should every child be able to do after ten or twelve years of schooling?
A modern curriculum should answer that question clearly. Students need more than subject knowledge. They should be able to think critically, solve unfamiliar problems, communicate clearly, work with others, adapt to change, learn independently and use technology responsibly. They need creativity and initiative, but also empathy, integrity and civic responsibility. They should acquire practical and technical skills while developing the ability to keep learning throughout life.
The government's stated goals already include several of these areas, such as creativity, employability, practical skills and future-oriented technology. The challenge is to turn these aspirations into clearly defined competencies and make sure they are taught across the curriculum rather than left to a few new subjects.
What matters in the classroom
The real test of the new reform will not be the number of new textbooks. It will be whether teachers are prepared before the new curriculum reaches their classrooms; whether schools have the space, equipment and learning materials needed for practical and collaborative work; and whether assessment rewards understanding, reasoning and application rather than memorization .
The government has said the reform will be supported by teacher guides, workbooks, remedial materials and video lessons. These resources can support both teachers and students, but their value will depend on timely delivery and effective use. In particular, teachers need practical guidance on how to use these materials to support classroom learning rather than simply adding more content to what they already teach.
Where teaching methods come in
How teachers teach matters as much as what they teach. A lesson does not have to rely entirely on explanation and note-taking. Teachers can ask questions, encourage short discussions, use simple classroom activities, give students problems to solve, and let them work together and explain their ideas. Such approaches can help students understand and apply what they learn rather than simply remember it. The aim is not to burden teachers with complicated new methods, but to gradually make classrooms more interactive and give students a more active role in learning.
Teachers can also use approaches such as the flipped classroom, project-based learning, and problem-based learning where they are appropriate. However, no single teaching method is suitable for every subject, every topic, or every learner. The choice should depend on what students are expected to learn and which approach is most likely to help them achieve that learning goal. A strong curriculum should therefore give teachers a repertoire of methods and, equally importantly, the training and resources to know when and how to use them.
The real test of reform
The goal should not be another curriculum that looks modern on paper but proves difficult to implement in practice. Nor should reform be reduced to adding new subjects, textbooks or digital materials. Its real measure is whether students leave school able to read and write well, think clearly, solve problems, communicate and collaborate, use technology wisely, adapt to change and act responsibly.
Bangladesh does not need to keep changing the destination. It needs to prepare its teachers, equip its schools and improve what happens in the classroom so that students can actually reach it. The challenge now is not to design another ambitious curriculum, but to build a reliable road from policy to the classroom.
MM Shahidul Hassan is d istinguished p rofessor, Eastern University, and f ormer v ice c hancellor, East West University, Bangladesh .

item.title: Four cigarette price tiers, 12 price points: A system designed for switching, not quitting
item.description:
When cigarette prices rise, smokers are expected to cut consumption or quit. That is the central public-health justification for increasing tobacco taxes. In Bangladesh, however, many smokers can respond in a much simpler way: They can switch to a cheaper brand.
A rapid survey conducted by PROGGA (Knowledge for Progress) in September 2026 shows how easily this can happen. The survey covered 80 cigarette retailers across all eight divisional cities and identified 53 brands being sold at 12 distinct price points.
Yet, officially, Bangladesh has only four cigarette price tiers: Low, medium, high, and premium.
This means that what appears to be a four-tier structure in government policy has become a 12-price-point market in practice. Such a wide range of prices gives smokers ample room to move down the price ladder when their preferred cigarettes become more expensive.
A major loophole in the low tier
The greatest price variation was found in the low tier, where cigarettes were available at eight different price points.
Under the current structure, the minimum retail prices for a pack of 10 cigarettes are Tk65 and above for the low tier, Tk92 and above for the medium tier, Tk160 and above for the high tier, and Tk210 and above for the premium tier.
The problem lies partly in the phrase “and above.”
If the low tier begins at Tk65 and the medium tier begins at Tk92, manufacturers can place low-tier cigarettes at several prices between Tk65 and Tk91. Indeed, the survey found a low-tier cigarette priced at Tk90, only Tk2 below the starting price of the medium tier.
Therefore, a smoker facing a price increase does not necessarily have to quit, reduce consumption or even move to another official tier. The smoker may simply switch to a slightly cheaper cigarette within the same tier.
This flexibility weakens the intended effect of tobacco taxation.
Cheap cigarettes remain widely available
Bangladesh already faces a major tobacco-use burden. According to the Global Adult Tobacco Survey 2017, 35.3% of adults used tobacco, while 18% smoked tobacco.
At the same time, cigarettes remain remarkably affordable. The WHO Report on the Global Tobacco Epidemic 2025 placed Bangladesh 163rd among 186 countries in terms of the price of the cheapest cigarette brand in 2024. In other words, Bangladesh remains among the countries where cheap cigarettes are most readily available.
The country also scored only 1.38 out of 5 in the fourth edition of the Cigarette Tax Scorecard, published in 2025. One reason for this poor performance is Bangladesh’s complex, multi-tiered ad valorem tax structure.
Under an ad valorem system, taxes are calculated as a percentage of the declared retail price. When numerous price points are available, cigarette companies can maintain cheaper brands and position products strategically across the market. Smokers who are sensitive to price can then switch brands rather than quit.
This is particularly concerning in a country where household incomes are limited and young people can access inexpensive cigarettes. The continued availability of very cheap brands undermines both public-health objectives and the effectiveness of tax increases.
Tax increases alone are not enough
Tobacco taxation is one of the most effective tools available for reducing tobacco consumption. But its effectiveness depends on more than the rate of tax.
The structure of the tax system matters just as much.
If taxes increase but cheaper alternatives remain widely available, many smokers will simply move down the price spectrum. This is known as down-trading. The more price points the market offers, the easier down-trading becomes.
The PROGGA survey provides a snapshot of how this mechanism operates in Bangladesh. With 53 brands spread across 12 price points, the cigarette market provides consumers with numerous alternatives at different levels of affordability.
As a result, a tax increase affecting one brand or price segment may not produce the expected reduction in cigarette consumption. It may merely redistribute smokers among brands.
A tax policy that raises the price of some cigarettes while leaving cheaper alternatives easily accessible cannot deliver its full public-health benefit.
Three reforms Bangladesh should pursue
The findings point to three urgent policy priorities.
First, the government should remove the phrase “and above” from cigarette price-tier definitions. As long as broad price ranges remain within each tier, manufacturers will be able to market cigarettes at multiple price points. Each tier should instead have a clearly specified retail price.
Second, Bangladesh should progressively reduce the number of cigarette price tiers, with the ultimate objective of introducing a single tier. A single price and tax tier would sharply reduce the opportunity to switch between cheaper and more expensive cigarettes.
Third, the country should move towards a simple, uniform specific excise tax. Under such a system, a fixed amount of tax would apply to each cigarette or pack, regardless of its retail price. The tax should be increased regularly so that cigarette prices rise faster than inflation and income growth.
This is essential because a nominal price increase does not automatically make cigarettes less affordable. If people’s incomes rise faster than cigarette prices, cigarettes may become more affordable over time, even after-tax increases.
Make all cigarettes less affordable
The objective of tobacco taxation should not be merely to make selected cigarette brands more expensive. It should be to make all cigarettes progressively less affordable and to leave consumers with fewer opportunities to avoid the intended impact of tax increases.
Bangladesh’s current system falls short of that objective.
Four official price tiers have produced at least 12 effective price points. The result is a market in which smokers can adjust their brand choices according to their ability to pay, instead of reducing consumption or quitting.
This is not simply a technical problem in tax administration. It is a public-health concern with consequences for families, healthcare expenditure and the country’s broader development.
Closing the price gaps, reducing the number of tiers and adopting a uniform specific tax would make the cigarette tax system simpler, more transparent and more effective. Most importantly, these reforms would help ensure that future tax increases lead to lower cigarette consumption rather than another round of brand switching.
ABM Zubair is Executive Director of PROGGA (Knowledge for Progress) and Director of the Centre for Research and Advocacy to Fight Tobacco (CRAFT), Bangladesh. Email: progga.bd@gmail.com .
